plan.contextChunk: This figure is a grouped vertical bar chart on a pale blue plotting field comparing two thermal properties of the straight-chain alkanes. The horizontal axis, labeled Number of carbons, carries fourteen categories numbered 1 through 14. The vertical axis, labeled Temperature (degrees C), runs from -200 at the bottom to 300 at the top with labeled gridlines every 100 degrees, and the bars grow upward or downward from the zero gridline. A legend in the upper left assigns blue to Melting point and magenta to Boiling point, and each carbon number carries one bar of each color, blue on the left and magenta on the right. Both series climb steadily from left to right. The blue melting-point bars begin near -180 at one carbon and stay below zero until the last two categories, where they finally reach and just cross the zero line. The magenta boiling-point bars start near -165, rise past zero at four carbons, and continue to roughly 250 at fourteen carbons. In every pair the magenta bar stands taller than the blue one, and the vertical gap between the two widens toward the right of the chart. The plot backs the observation that both transition temperatures increase with molecular size, since the dispersion forces holding molecules together grow as the chain lengthens.

interactionPlan.concept: Both the melting point and boiling point of straight-chain alkanes rise steadily as the carbon chain lengthens, because longer chains have larger surface area and therefore stronger London dispersion forces holding the molecules together.

demo_steps.narration: Each carbon number carries a blue melting-point bar and a taller magenta boiling-point bar; both series climb from left to right as the chain grows.

demo_steps.title: Sweep the chain length
demo_steps.narration: Drag the carbon slider toward C14 and watch the highlighted pair's temperatures climb: stronger dispersion forces in longer chains raise both the melting and boiling points.

demo_steps.title: Boiling point crosses zero early
demo_steps.narration: With boiling point emphasized, note it passes 0 °C already near C4 and keeps rising to about 250 °C at C14, always staying above the melting point.

demo_steps.title: Melting point lags behind
demo_steps.narration: Switch emphasis to melting point: the blue bars stay negative until the longest chains, finally reaching and just crossing 0 °C only around C13-C14, showing melting points rise more slowly and remain below boiling points throughout.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Longer alkane chains mean more surface contact and stronger London dispersion forces, so both melting and boiling points increase with carbon number — with the boiling point always higher and crossing 0 °C at far shorter chains than the melting point.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Grouped vertical bars on a pale blue field. X-axis 'Number of carbons' with categories 1-14; Y-axis 'Temperature (°C)' from -200 to 300 with gridlines every 100 and a clear zero line. In each group the blue (melting) bar sits left and the magenta (boiling) bar right; magenta is always taller. Approximate melting values: C1 -182, C2 -183, C3 -190, C4 -138, C5 -130, C6 -95, C7 -91, C8 -57, C9 -51, C10 -30, C11 -26, C12 -10, C13 -5, C14 +5. Approximate boiling values: C1 -164, C2 -89, C3 -42, C4 -1, C5 +36, C6 +69, C7 +98, C8 +126, C9 +151, C10 +174, C11 +196, C12 +216, C13 +235, C14 +254. Legend top-left with blue and magenta swatches. The slider highlights the selected pair (e.g. thicker outline plus small temperature labels above each bar); the toggle dims the non-emphasized series to a faded tint while keeping it as reference. Bars grow up or down from the zero gridline.

authoredContext:
Alkanes show regular increases in both boiling point and melting point as molecular weight increases (the figure), an effect due to the presence of weak dispersion forces between molecules (another section). Only when sufficient energy is applied to overcome these forces does the solid melt or liquid boil. As you might expect, dispersion forces increase as molecular size increases, accounting for the higher melting and boiling points of larger alkanes.

A plot of melting and boiling points versus number of carbon atoms for the C1–C14 straight-chain alkanes. There is a regular increase with molecular size.

A double bar graph of temperature versus the number of carbon atoms that plots bars for melting and boiling points with an increasing trend.

Another effect seen in alkanes is that increased branching lowers an alkane’s boiling point. Thus, pentane has no branches and boils at 36.1 °C, isopentane (2-methylbutane) has one branch and boils at 27.85 °C, and neopentane (2,2-dimethylpropane) has two branches and boils at 9.5 °C. Similarly, octane boils at 125.7 °C, whereas isooctane (2,2,4-trimethylpentane) boils at 99.3 °C. Branched-chain alkanes are lower-boiling because they are more nearly spherical than straight-chain alkanes, have smaller surface areas, and consequently have smaller dispersion forces.

discrepancies: The default (step-0) view is not a clean drop-in for the static source: it draws a black-outlined highlighted bar pair at C1 plus on-bar value labels ('-182 °C', '-164 °C') that the source figure does not contain.
The source y-axis shows minor tick marks/gridlines at 50 °C intervals between the labeled 100 °C lines; the generated chart only renders major gridlines every 100 °C.
The legend sits in a strip above the plot area, whereas the source places the colored-square legend inside the plot at the top-left.
The two value labels on the highlighted pair crowd together at the extreme negative end (C1), nearly colliding near the bottom axis.
evaluation.notes: Bars, axis ranges, series colors, and the underlying melting/boiling data all match the source and the slider/emphasis/step-player interactions are functional and on-concept, but the step-0 state adds a highlight outline and value labels the clean source lacks, the legend is moved outside the plot, and 50 °C minor ticks are missing.
action_items: Make the initial render a faithful static match: start with no highlighted bar (no black border) and no on-bar value labels, and only introduce the highlight/labels once the user moves the slider or advances a step.
Add minor y-axis ticks/gridlines at 50 °C intervals (e.g. a secondary tick set or afterBuildTicks) to mirror the source's finer gridline spacing.
Position the legend inside the chart area at the top-left (Chart.js legend with align/position tweaks or a custom HTML overlay) to match the source composition.
Improve the collision-aware label offsets so the melting and boiling value labels never overlap at the extreme negative end (C1-C3).

feedback.rationale: No failure modes, all scores at 4–5, and the remaining discrepancies are minor polish details (initial-state highlight, minor gridlines, legend position) that do not materially affect the figure's correctness or usability.
